The text describes diethylstilbestrol (DES) as a 'trans-placental acting carcinogen' and notes that mice treated neonatally or in utero with DES show morphological abnormalities of the female reproductive tract similar to those associated with disruption of the WNT signaling pathway.

The passage notes that while many compounds act as anti-progressors (e.g., danazol for breast tumour, cysteamine for glandular stomach tumour, mitomycin-C for bladder tumours in rodents), only a few compounds have been found to act as progressor agents in multistep carcinogenesis: diethylstilbestrol, benzene, asbestos, potassium arsenide, and ionizing radiation (UVB and UVC), citing Pitot and Gragan (1991).
